prompt: Hand-inked graphic novel character model sheet, clean confident ink outlines, flat cel shading in a muted sun-faded palette, plain cream paper background, no floor, no ground line, no shadows, no text. The same boy drawn four times in one row at exactly the same scale: front view, side profile facing right, back view, side profile facing left. Strict orthographic views, relaxed standing pose with arms slightly away from the body, feet slightly apart. He is an original 15-year-old caboclo boy, an apprentice raft fisherman in Fortaleza, Ceará, in 1932, of strong Indigenous heritage mixed with African and Portuguese: a broad face with high, prominent cheekbones, dark almond-shaped eyes, thick straight dark eyebrows, a broad nose, full lips, a firm jaw; thick, straight, coarse black hair cut short and uneven; warm bronze-brown skin deeply tanned by sun and sea; lean and wiry, lanky, long limbs, big hands and big bare feet; a real teenager, not a child, a grounded serious-but-warm look. Clothes like the Fortaleza fishermen in photographs from the 1930s: a close-fitting knitted cotton jersey shirt with wide horizontal stripes of faded brick red and off-white, sleeves to the elbow, worn and slightly stretched; loose light off-white cotton trousers rolled up to mid-shin, plain, with no back pockets; a narrow belt of worn dark-brown raw leather with a small darkened-iron buckle; a dark faded indigo cloth knotted around his LEFT upper arm; barefoot; a woven palm-straw hat with a tall crown and a wide soft brim, a little too big for him.
